540.title: Chitrakoot
540.hook: you can still walk barefoot around the hill where the exiles lived
540.carry: reading the story with your feet
540.howItsDone: Pilgrims at Chitrakoot bathe at Ram Ghat on the Mandakini and walk the parikrama, the circuit around Kamadgiri hill, often barefoot, especially on new-moon days.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chitrakoot, the bright mountain, and your line, a parnashala, a house of leaves. Valmiki welcomed the exiles into his own story.

Most stories happen in places you can't go. Nobody can buy a ticket to Middle-earth. But on the border of Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh there's a small town called Chitrakoot, with a green hill, a river and a lot of temples. Every day pilgrims arrive, take off their shoes, and start walking around the hill where, they believe, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana once lived in a hut of leaves.
screen: `PLACES YOU CAN'T GO.` → `A TOWN CALLED CHITRAKOOT.` → `PILGRIMS TAKE OFF THEIR SHOES.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Chitra means bright, wonderful, many-colored; kuta means a peak. The bright peak. In Hindi it's usually said Chitrakoot. Valmiki names a river there, the Mandakini, and it still runs through the town. Its main bathing place is Ram Ghat, where in the evenings people float lamps on the water. The hill at the center is Kamadgiri, often explained as the hill that grants wishes. Pilgrims walk all the way around it, often barefoot, stopping at shrines on the path. Walking around something holy, keeping it on your right, is called parikrama, and Hindus honor temples, rivers and hills this way. There's another layer. Chitrakoot is linked with the poet Tulsidas, who retold the Ramayana in Hindi, and a well-known tradition says that at Ram Ghat he was granted a vision of Rama. So the town carries two Ramayanas at once, Valmiki's Sanskrit and Tulsidas's Hindi. For pilgrims, the Ramayana isn't only a book. Its places are real places, and walking them is reading the story with your feet. Scholars debate which modern sites match which verses, and the text doesn't settle every question. The pilgrims aren't waiting for them. Every morning, they take off their shoes and walk.
screen: `CHITRA AND KUTA: THE BRIGHT PEAK.` · `THE MANDAKINI AND RAM GHAT.` · `KAMADGIRI AND THE PARIKRAMA.` · `TULSIDAS'S VISION AT RAM GHAT.` · then, large: `READING THE STORY WITH YOUR FEET.`

541.title: Chitrakoot
541.hook: Rama walks Sita around the mountain and tells her he doesn't miss the kingdom at all
541.tomorrow: Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it (Shravana Kumara)
541.howItsDone: In the text, the Mandakini at Chitrakuta is where Rama and Sita bathe; pilgrims to Chitrakoot bathe in the same river today.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chitrakoot today, a pilgrim town, and your line, reading the story with your feet. People still walk barefoot around Kamadgiri.

Every hard story has a pause, a stretch where the characters simply get to live. On Chitrakuta, the exiles get theirs. The hut is built. The days fall into a rhythm: bathing in the river, gathering fruit, sitting by the fire at night. And one day Rama takes Sita by the hand and walks her around the mountain, pointing things out, the way you'd show someone a neighborhood you've just moved into and already love.
screen: `EVERY HARD STORY HAS A PAUSE.` → `A RHYTHM TO THE DAYS.` → `SHOWING HER THE NEIGHBORHOOD.`

segments.voice: Look at the peaks, Rama tells Sita: some silver, some red, some gold, some the color of crystal. Look at the waterfalls, the flowering trees, the birds. Then he says something tender. Seeing this mountain with you, I don't grieve for the kingdom, and I don't miss my friends. Living here brings him two good things: he keeps his father's word, and he gives his brother Bharata joy. He takes her down to the Mandakini. The water is clear. Sages bathe in it, raising their arms to the sun, and deer come down to drink. Bathe here with me, he says. Think of this mountain as Ayodhya, the deer as its people, and the Mandakini as our own river Sarayu. You might hear an echo. Sumitra told Lakshmana: think of the forest as Ayodhya. Now Rama says it to Sita, and on the mountain, it's true. One honest note. Valmiki actually tells this scene a little later, while trouble is already on its way, and the contrast is part of his art. We've placed it here because it's the clearest picture of those first days. Now back to where Valmiki's story runs next. Far away, the charioteer Sumantra is driving into Ayodhya, alone, with an empty chariot. And an old king is waiting.
screen: `SILVER, RED AND GOLDEN PEAKS.` · `I DON'T GRIEVE FOR THE KINGDOM.` · `THE MANDAKINI IS OUR SARAYU.` · `THE CAMERA TURNS TO AYODHYA.` · then, large: `AN EMPTY CHARIOT GOES HOME.`

542.title: Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it (Shravana Kumara)
542.hook: an empty chariot comes home, and an old king finally tells a secret he has carried his whole life
542.tomorrow: Dasharatha's death and the curse that, part two
542.howItsDone: Ramayana reciters often tell Dasharatha's confession as its own episode, and later tellings know the young man as Shravan Kumar, in a children's story about care for parents.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chitrakoot, the happy pause, and your line, a hut on the hill. Rama told Sita the mountain was their Ayodhya now.

Sumantra drives back into Ayodhya alone. The horses hang their heads. People look past him into the empty chariot, and then the wailing starts. He gives the king Rama's messages, one by one, and Dasharatha sinks deeper into grief. That night, lying beside Kausalya, unable to sleep, he starts to talk. Not about Rama. About himself, long ago, when he was young and very good with a bow.
screen: `AN EMPTY CHARIOT COMES HOME.` → `THE KING CAN'T SLEEP.` → `A STORY FROM LONG AGO.`

segments.voice: He begins with a saying: whatever a person does, good or bad, they eat its fruit later. Then he tells Kausalya what he has never told her. Before they were married, as a prince, he was famous for one skill. He could hit a target he couldn't see, just by its sound. The Sanskrit word for an archer like that is shabdavedhi, one who pierces by sound. One rainy season, he went out at night along the Sarayu, hoping to catch an elephant or a buffalo coming down to drink. It was dark. He heard a deep gurgling at the water's edge, and was sure it was an elephant. He fitted an arrow, aimed at the sound, and let go. From the water came a human cry, and a question. Who would shoot at someone like me? I live in the forest, I harm no one, I only came for water. The prince ran to the bank. Half in the river lay a young ascetic with matted hair, an arrow in his chest, and beside him a water pot, the thing that had made the sound. Dasharatha tells Kausalya he was shaking, his mind gone dark. A skill he was proud of, a guess in the dark, a shot that can't be called back. He has carried it since he was young, and tonight, with his son gone, he finally says it out loud.
screen: `WHAT YOU DO, YOU EAT LATER.` · `SHABDAVEDHI: HE SHOOTS AT SOUND.` · `A SOUND HE TOOK FOR AN ELEPHANT.` · `A WATER POT, AND A YOUNG ASCETIC.` · then, large: `ONE SHOT THAT CAN'T BE CALLED BACK.`

543.title: Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it (Shravana Kumara)
543.word: Dasharatha's death and the curse that
543.hook: a prince carries a water pot to a hut where two blind parents are waiting for their son
543.carry: Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it (Shravana Kumara)
543.tomorrow: Dasharatha's death and the curse that, part three
543.howItsDone: This episode is often told on its own as a story about duty to parents, and about a prince who told a blind couple the truth instead of slipping away.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shabdavedhi, an archer who shoots at sound. The young prince shot at a sound in the dark and found a young ascetic with a water pot.

The young man in the river doesn't curse Dasharatha. That's the first surprise. He's dying, and what he talks about is his parents. They're old, and both blind, sitting in a hut nearby, thirsty, waiting for me to bring water. Go to them. Tell them. Then he asks one more thing: pull out the arrow. It's burning. The prince knows that if he pulls it, the boy will die. He does it anyway, because he was asked.
screen: `HE DOESN'T CURSE THE PRINCE.` → `MY PARENTS ARE BLIND AND THIRSTY.` → `PULL OUT THE ARROW.`

segments.voice: So Dasharatha fills the pot and walks the path the boy described. At the hut, the old father hears footsteps and speaks first. Why are you so late, son? Your mother was worried. Did we upset you? Say something. Picture the prince standing there with the water, mistaken for the son he has just killed. This is the moment the episode turns on. Nobody saw. He could set the pot down and slip away. Instead he tells them everything: who he is, the sound, the elephant he imagined, the arrow. In Valmiki's telling, the father answers with something striking. Because you told us yourself, you are still alive. Had you hidden it, far worse would have followed. The confession doesn't undo the death, but it changes what follows. The parents ask to be taken to their son. They sit with his body by the river, touching his face, grieving aloud. Then the father speaks the words that will shape Dasharatha's life. Just as I am losing my life in grief for my son, you too will one day die grieving for a son. And the old couple give up their lives on their son's funeral fire. Hold both halves. Telling the truth spared the young prince that night. It didn't spare him the curse. And tonight, with Rama gone and his own life fading, the old king tells Kausalya the curse is coming true.

544.title: Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it (Shravana Kumara)
544.hook: a king dies at midnight, and a boy with no name in the oldest text becomes one of India's best-known sons
544.howItsDone: Shravan Kumar is a common children's story across much of India, told to teach care for parents, and his name is still used as praise for a devoted son or daughter.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it. You too will die grieving for a son, the blind father said. The truth spared the prince that night, but not the curse.
screen: `YOU TOO WILL GRIEVE FOR A SON.`

segments.voice: In many Indian homes, children hear about the young man at the river long before anyone reads them the Ramayana. In those tellings he has a name, Shravan Kumar, and a picture: a son carrying his blind parents on pilgrimage, one in each of two baskets hung from a pole across his shoulders. Grandparents tell it at bedtime as the story of a good son. Here's the surprise. In Valmiki's Ramayana, the young man has no name, and there are no baskets. Both came later.
screen: `A NAME CHILDREN KNOW.` → `TWO BASKETS ON A POLE.` → `IN VALMIKI, NO NAME.`

segments.voice: First, the night ends. Dasharatha finishes the story, and he knows what it means. The curse is arriving. He tells Kausalya his eyes are failing; he can't see her anymore. If only Rama would come back and touch me now, he says. He names the people lucky enough to see Rama's face when he returns. And somewhere past midnight, still speaking of his son, the old king dies. In the morning the singers and attendants come to wake him, as always, and find him gone. The palace breaks into grief. No son is there for the last rites: Rama is in the forest, and Bharata far away in his grandfather's kingdom. So the ministers do something unusual. They lay the king's body in a vessel of oil, to keep it until Bharata comes. Messengers ride for Kekaya with strict orders: say nothing. Just bring him. Now the name. Valmiki calls the boy simply the young ascetic, the hermit's son. Later retellings, in regional languages and folk tradition, call him Shravana, or Shravan Kumar, and add the baskets and the pilgrimage. The name fits oddly well. Shravana is a Sanskrit word connected with hearing, and this boy was killed by an archer who shot at a sound. So the story grew, over the centuries, around the one detail Valmiki left open, and a boy with no name became a byword for loving your parents.

545.title: Bharata's journey
545.hook: a prince wakes from a bad dream, and riders arrive who won't tell him why they've come
545.howItsDone: Ramayana reciters tell Bharata's homecoming as its own episode: the dream, the silent city, and his first question, for Rama rather than the throne.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shravana, the name later tellings gave the boy at the river. The old king died past midnight, and riders left for Kekaya, saying nothing.

Far away, in his grandfather's city, Bharata wakes up badly shaken. His friends try music and jokes, and he can't smile. He tells them his dream. His father, pale, hair loose, smeared with oil, riding a chariot pulled by donkeys, heading south. In the epics, the south is the direction of Yama, the lord of death. Bharata says: either I, or Rama, or Lakshmana, or the king is going to die. That same day, the riders from Ayodhya arrive.
screen: `A DREAM IN KEKAYA.` → `A CHARIOT HEADING SOUTH.` → `THE RIDERS ARRIVE.`

segments.voice: The messengers do exactly as they were told. Your family's priest sends greetings, they say. There's urgent business. Come at once. Bharata asks after everyone, one by one: his father, Rama, Lakshmana, the three queens. The messengers give polite answers that aren't quite answers. All is well with those you ask about. So he takes leave of his grandfather and sets out. Valmiki gives us the road, the rivers crossed, the towns passed, days of it. Then Ayodhya appears, and something is wrong. No music. No crowds. The gardens look neglected, the people avoid his eyes. This isn't my city, Bharata tells the charioteer. He goes to his father's rooms, and his father isn't there. So he goes to his mother. Kaikeyi is glad to see him. She asks about the journey, about her family. Then she tells him, almost lightly: your father has gone the way all living things go. Bharata falls to the floor. When he can speak, he asks: where is Rama? I want to touch his feet. He's my father now. And Kaikeyi, sure she's giving good news, tells him the rest: the two boons, the exile, the throne kept for him. She thinks she's made her son a king. She has no idea what she's about to hear.

546.title: Bharata's journey
546.hook: the son a mother schemed for turns on her, and then has to convince another mother he never wanted any of it
546.howItsDone: Bharata is honored in Ramayana tradition as a model of loyalty and renunciation; his oaths before Kausalya run on for many verses of the Ayodhya Kanda.

segments.voice: Yesterday: your line, she thinks it's good news. Bharata came home to a silent city, and Kaikeyi told him the throne was his.

Kaikeyi has been waiting for this conversation: her son home, the crown ready. What she gets is fury. Bharata doesn't thank her. He tells her she has destroyed the family, killed his father with grief, and sent away the brother he loves. The kingdom she won for him, he says, he will never accept. Then he walks out, to face the person he dreads most: Kausalya, Rama's mother.
screen: `NO THANKS, ONLY GRIEF.` → `I WILL NEVER ACCEPT IT.` → `NOW, KAUSALYA.`

segments.voice: Kausalya has every reason to suspect him. Here is the son who gains everything from her son's exile. She says so, bitterly: you wanted the kingdom, now you have it. Take me to Rama too. Bharata falls at her feet and swears. Valmiki gives him a long chain of oaths, each naming a wrong he'd rather be guilty of than this. May I carry the guilt of one who betrays a trust, who strikes a sleeping person, who turns away a guest, if I ever wanted Rama gone. On and on, a son emptying himself out. Kausalya believes him. She takes his head in her lap, and they weep together. Then the duty that can't wait. Under Vasishtha's guidance, Bharata performs his father's funeral rites. The body is taken from the oil, the fire is lit, the queens and the city mourn, and the family offers water at the Sarayu. Afterward, at the palace, Shatrughna catches Manthara, the maid who started it all, and starts to drag her. Bharata stops him: Rama would never forgive us. And so the week closes. A hut on a green hill. A king's confession: a sound in the dark, a water pot, a father's curse. A death past midnight. A boy with no name who became Shravan Kumar. And a son called home without being told, who refuses the prize.

segments.voice: Think of a time someone suspected you of something you didn't do, or you suspected someone who turned out innocent, and notice where it sits in your body: the jaw, the chest, the stomach. Breathe into that spot, and let each out-breath loosen it a little, the way Kausalya's suspicion loosened.
